# 🖥️ EasyTrade — Kubernetes Capacity & Efficiency Review
*How well are the `local-wsl-capstone` cluster's resource requests match actual usage, and is there any capacity or stability risk worth flagging?*

Sourced from Kubernetes container metrics and Smartscape pod configuration.

## CPU Efficiency by Workload
Efficiency = actual CPU usage ÷ requested CPU. Low numbers mean a workload is requesting far more CPU than it uses — cluster capacity reserved but sitting idle. **`easytrade-db` is the standout: only 4.2% CPU efficiency**, requesting 500m but using ~21m. Several other workloads (calculationservice, frontend, pricing-service) sit under 20% — CPU requests across the fleet look sized for a much heavier peak load than this environment sees today.

input.value:
timeseries {usage = avg(dt.kubernetes.container.cpu_usage, scalar:true), requests = avg(dt.kubernetes.container.requests_cpu, scalar:true)}, by:{k8s.workload.name, k8s.namespace.name}
| filter k8s.namespace.name == "easytrade" and requests > 0
| fieldsAdd efficiency_pct = round(usage * 100.0 / requests, decimals:1)
| fields k8s.workload.name, efficiency_pct
| sort efficiency_pct asc

sections.markdown:
## Memory Efficiency by Workload
Memory tells a much healthier story than CPU — most workloads sit between 29% and 80% of their requested memory, a normal range with reasonable headroom rather than gross over-provisioning. This asymmetry (tight memory sizing, loose CPU sizing) suggests teams sized requests for memory safety margins first and left CPU requests at a generic default.

input.value:
timeseries {usage = avg(dt.kubernetes.container.memory_working_set, scalar:true), requests = avg(dt.kubernetes.container.requests_memory, scalar:true)}, by:{k8s.workload.name, k8s.namespace.name}
| filter k8s.namespace.name == "easytrade" and requests > 0
| fieldsAdd efficiency_pct = round(usage * 100.0 / requests, decimals:1)
| fields k8s.workload.name, efficiency_pct
| sort efficiency_pct asc

sections.markdown:
## Configuration Hygiene — Resource Limits
A quick governance check: does every container in the `easytrade` namespace have both a CPU and memory limit configured? **Yes — the query below returns zero rows**, confirming full coverage. That's a genuinely good sign; missing limits is one of the most common causes of noisy-neighbor CPU starvation and unbounded memory growth in a shared cluster.

input.value:
smartscapeNodes "K8S_POD"
| filter k8s.namespace.name == "easytrade"
| parse k8s.object, "JSON:config"
| expand container = config[spec][containers]
| fieldsAdd container_name = container[name], cpu_limit = container[resources][limits][cpu], mem_limit = container[resources][limits][memory]
| filter isNull(cpu_limit) or isNull(mem_limit)
| summarize count(), by:{container_name}

sections.title: Containers Missing a CPU or Memory Limit

## Container Restarts & OOM History
Restart and out-of-memory-kill trend — widen the time range to 7 or 30 days to see the historical incidents (this environment saw 27 restarts and 19 OOM kills over the trailing month, none in the last 2 hours).

sections.title: Container Restarts & OOM Kills Over Time

sections.markdown:
## Takeaways
- **Right-size CPU requests**, especially `easytrade-db`, `easytrade-calculationservice`, and `easytrade-frontend` — all under 20% CPU efficiency. Lowering their requests would free real scheduling capacity on this single-node cluster.
- **Memory sizing is healthy** — no action needed there.
- **Resource-limit hygiene is clean** — every container has both limits set; keep this as a standard for any new service added to the namespace.
- **Widen the time range on the restarts/OOM chart** to see the historical incident pattern; nothing is happening right now, but the 30-day history is worth reviewing alongside the Incident & Reliability Retrospective notebook.
